The effigy is placed on top of an altar tomb lined with 22 pleurants (or "weepers"), who are also dressed in armour.

Alexander Stewart, the Wolf of Badenoch
Stuart was the third surviving son  son of king Robert II of Scotland (1316 – 1390). He is known to history as the deeply unpopular "Wolf of Badenoch", a name given due to  his notorious cruelty, in particular for his destruction of the royal burgh of Elgin and its 13th-century cathedral in May 1370, for which he earned a reputation as "an enemy of the Church", and was described in 2017 as "Scothland's vilest man".

Description
The tomb is inscribed with the year 1420.The monument remains in its origional position behind the choir screen at the east-end of the cathedral, while Stuart's grave is underneath.

Effigy
The effigy is made from grey–green marble and measures 7 ft (2.1 m) in length. Stewart lies on a cloak and is dressed in full armour with his sword by his left slide. His head is protected by a bascinet (an open-faced combat helmet) and visor and he wears a pauldron—a type of spaulder covering the shoulders. He has a breastplate over his torso, above a plate-skirt at his hips. He has a hip-belt of a type worn in Scotland until the end of the 15th century.The animal resting at his feet may be a lion, or—less likely—a dog.
The effigy is in poor condition, having been damaged c. 1560 during the Scottish Reformation. It now consists of four separate pieces having been broken apart at the neck, waist, knees and ankles. His right foot is missing and his face and left foot are severely damaged. However, it remains one of the best preserved pieces of royal medieval Scottish sculpture.

Altar tomb
The altar (or "chest") tomb contains 22 pleurants (or "weepers", that is sculpted figures representing mourners) dressed in armour; eight on each long-side and three at each end. These figures are positioned under three-arch canopies and separated by small buttresses.The Latin inscription is placed on the edge of the stone slab below the effigy. It reads, "His Jacet Domninus Alexander Senescallus, Dominus De Badenoch, Bonæ Memorle, Qui Obit 24 Die Mensis Julii, Anno Domini 1394".

## Kisah Terendam Gas: Tragedi Sheffield Musim Dingin 2022

Musim dingin di Sheffield, Inggris, selalu membawa hawa dingin yang menusuk tulang, tetapi Desember 2022 akan dikenang sebagai musim yang mengejutkan dan menguji ketahanan ribuan keluarga. Mari kita telusuri apa yang terjadi, mengapa, dan bagaimana kota itu bangkit.

Malam tanggal 2 Desember terasa seperti malam musim dingin biasa di Stannington, sebuah distrik di barat laut Sheffield. Namun, di bawah tanah yang beku, sebuah masalah serius mulai muncul. Sebuah pipa utama air tanah di Bankfield Lane, yang sudah berusia puluhan tahun sejak dipasang pada tahun 1970-an, tiba-tiba **pecah**. Bayangkan sebuah retakan besar, cukup untuk memuntahkan lebih dari 2 juta liter air — itu setara dengan tiga kolam renang ukuran Olimpiade!

Awalnya, ini mungkin terdengar seperti masalah air biasa. Namun, apa yang terjadi selanjutnya adalah skenario yang tidak pernah dibayangkan siapa pun.

### Sumber Masalah: Invasi Air ke Jaringan Gas

**Penyebab utama pemadaman pasokan gas ini adalah air yang membanjiri jaringan pipa gas alam.** Ya, Anda tidak salah dengar. Air dari pipa utama yang pecah itu tidak hanya membanjiri jalanan, tetapi entah bagaimana menemukan jalan masuk ke dalam sistem pipa gas bawah tanah.

Bagaimana ini bisa terjadi? Air mengalir dengan deras, menuruni lereng bukit, dan karena tekanan dan mungkin adanya celah atau titik lemah di kedua sistem, ia berhasil masuk ke dalam jaringan gas Cadent Gas. Ini adalah peristiwa yang “belum pernah terjadi sebelumnya,” seperti yang digambarkan oleh Cadent Gas sendiri.

Aparat darurat mulai bergerak sekitar tengah malam, mengetuk pintu-pintu rumah untuk membangunkan warga, menyadari bahwa ini bukan hanya sekadar banjir biasa. Air mulai meluap dari meteran gas dan kompor gas di dalam rumah warga, bahkan dari penutup lubang got dan dasar lampu jalan di luar. Ini adalah indikasi yang jelas bahwa jaringan gas telah terkompromi secara serius.

### Dampak Berantai: Kehilangan Segala Kenyamanan Modern

Pada tanggal 3 Desember, lebih dari 1.000 properti sudah tanpa pasokan gas. Ini berarti:

*   **Tanpa Pemanas Sentral:** Di tengah musim dingin, suhu beku menjadi ancaman nyata.
*   **Tanpa Kompor Gas:** Memasak menjadi tantangan besar.
*   **Masalah Air dan Listrik:** Sebagai efek domino, beberapa properti juga mengalami pemadaman air, dan karena banyak yang beralih ke pemanas listrik, jaringan listrik (Northern Powergrid) juga menjadi terbebani, menyebabkan pemadaman listrik sporadis di beberapa area.

Daerah yang paling parah terkena dampak adalah distrik Hillsborough, Malin Bridge, dan Stannington. Jumlah properti yang terdampak terus meningkat, mencapai lebih dari 2.000 pada tanggal 6 Desember, terutama rumah-rumah yang berada lebih rendah di lereng bukit di area Hillsborough.

### Upaya Pemulihan yang Masif dan Penuh Tantangan

Para insinyur dari Cadent Gas segera dikerahkan. Namun, tugasnya sangat besar dan rumit:

1.  **Mematikan Gas Satu Per Satu:** Mereka harus pergi dari pintu ke pintu untuk mematikan pasokan gas di setiap properti yang terdampak sebelum pekerjaan perbaikan bisa dimulai.
2.  **Menguras Air dari Pipa Gas:** Ini bukan hanya sekadar menguras genangan air biasa. Mereka harus memompa jutaan liter air dari jaringan pipa gas yang kompleks. Awalnya lebih dari 100 insinyur bekerja 24 jam sehari, kemudian meningkat menjadi lebih dari 200 insinyur, bahkan dibantu oleh personil dan peralatan dari seluruh negeri.
3.  **Cuaca Ekstrem:** Hujan lebat di awal menghambat pekerjaan, diikuti oleh suhu dingin yang ekstrem dan bahkan salju, dengan suhu mencapai -3°C pada 9 Desember. Kondisi cuaca semakin mempersulit warga dan tim pemulihan.

Pada tanggal 7 Desember, setelah hampir seminggu tanpa gas dan dengan ribuan properti masih terkena dampak, **Dewan Kota Sheffield secara resmi menyatakan “insiden besar” (major incident).** Deklarasi ini memungkinkan koordinasi dan pengerahan sumber daya yang lebih baik untuk mengatasi krisis.

Meskipun banyak rumah yang mulai tersambung kembali pada tanggal 10 Desember (sekitar tiga perempat properti), beberapa rumah di area Hillsborough dan Malin Bridge masih menghadapi kesulitan besar dalam pengurasan air, sehingga mereka tetap tanpa gas.

**Pemadaman pasokan gas ini berlangsung hampir selama DUA MINGGU** untuk beberapa properti. Bayangkan hidup tanpa pemanas atau kompor di tengah musim dingin selama hampir dua minggu!

Melihat skala krisis, komunitas Sheffield menunjukkan solidaritas yang luar biasa:

*   **Pusat Pengungsian:** Pemerintah daerah dan bisnis lokal membuka "ruang perlindungan" yang hangat, menyediakan makanan dan minuman panas.
*   **Bantuan Palang Merah:** Palang Merah mendistribusikan bantuan seperti makanan, minuman, dan selimut kepada warga yang terdampak.
*   **Sekolah Tetap Buka:** Sekolah-sekolah di area terdampak tetap buka, menggunakan pemanas listrik portabel di setiap kelas, meskipun dapur mereka tidak bisa berfungsi.
*   **Semangat Komunitas:** Warga saling membantu, dan para pejabat memuji ketahanan dan "semangat komunitas" yang mereka tunjukkan.

Yorkshire Water, penyedia air, mengeluarkan permintaan maaf. Mereka dikritik keras oleh warga yang marah, yang menuduh mereka tidak melakukan pemeliharaan yang memadai pada pipa air. Warga mengklaim ada hingga sepuluh pipa utama air yang pecah di area Stannington sebelum insiden besar ini.

Cadent Gas menjanjikan kompensasi untuk penggunaan listrik tambahan, dan kemudian mengkonfirmasi bahwa warga akan menerima dua kali lipat tingkat kompensasi biasa untuk pemadaman gas, total £910 untuk pemadaman tujuh hari.

### Pelajaran yang Dipetik

Kisah pemadaman gas di Sheffield ini memberikan beberapa pelajaran penting:

1.  **Infrastruktur yang Renta:** Sistem infrastruktur lama, seperti pipa air yang berusia puluhan tahun, memerlukan pemeliharaan yang cermat dan berkelanjutan untuk mencegah bencana.
2.  **Efek Domino:** Satu kegagalan di satu sistem (air) dapat menyebabkan efek domino yang menghancurkan pada sistem lain (gas, listrik), menunjukkan bahwa semua infrastruktur saling terkait.
3.  **Ketahanan Komunitas:** Dalam menghadapi krisis, solidaritas dan semangat komunitas sangatlah penting.
4.  **Kesiapan Darurat:** Pemerintah daerah dan dinas darurat perlu memiliki rencana kontingensi yang kuat untuk insiden besar yang tidak terduga.

Pemadaman gas di Sheffield pada Desember 2022 adalah pengingat nyata tentang betapa kita sangat bergantung pada infrastruktur modern dan bagaimana kegagalannya dapat memengaruhi kehidupan sehari-hari secara drastis. Ini juga merupakan kisah tentang bagaimana sebuah komunitas dapat bersatu untuk mengatasi kesulitan yang luar biasa.

{"metric":"geval_fluency","model":"google/gemini-2.5-flash","system_prompt":"Pembuatan cerita dari teks berikut: Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: When was GPT-4 released and what are some of its capabilities?","user_input":"Baik, mari kita selami dunia GPT-4 yang menakjubkan melalui sebuah cerita edukatif!

***

**Misteri di Balik Layar Kecerdasan Buatan**

Mentari pagi menelusup dari celah jendela, membangunkan Maya dari tidurnya. Gadis berusia 16 tahun itu menguap sambil meraih ponselnya. Notifikasi dari grup Diskusi Teknologi Sekolah memenuhi layarnya.

“Guys, ada yang sudah dengar tentang GPT-4?” ketik Kevin, teman sekelasnya.

“GPT-4? Apa itu makanan baru?” canda Dini.

Maya tersenyum. Dini memang selalu begitu. Tangannya bergerak cepat mengetik balasan. “Bukan, Dini! Itu singkatan dari Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4. Sebenarnya, ini adalah model bahasa raksasa terbaru dari OpenAI.”

Kevin membalas dengan emoji penasaran. “Serius? Lebih canggih dari ChatGPT yang biasa kita pakai ngerjain tugas biologi itu?”

“Tentu saja!” Maya segera menelepon Kevin dan Dini ke dalam panggilan grup. “Aku baru saja membaca artikel menarik. Kalian tahu ChatGPT yang kita pakai itu dibangun di atas GPT-3.5, kan? Nah, GPT-4 ini adalah penerusnya yang jauh lebih cerdas.”

“Lebih cerdas bagaimana?” tanya Dini, suaranya terdengar antusias.

“Kalian ingat GPT-1, model pertama yang diperkenalkan OpenAI tahun 2018? Itu masih sangat dasar, hanya bisa melatih pemahaman bahasa dari buku-buku. Lalu GPT-2 di 2019 yang bisa nulis teks lebih masuk akal. Dan GPT-3 di 2020, yang parameternya 100 kali lipat dari GPT-2 dan bisa melakukan banyak tugas dengan sedikit contoh,” jelas Maya, intonasinya seperti seorang profesor muda.

Kevin menyela, “Jadi, GPT-4 ini seperti evolusi puncak dari semua itu?”

“Kurang lebih begitu!” Maya mengangguk, meskipun tidak terlihat oleh teman-temannya. “**GPT-4 dirilis pada tanggal 14 Maret 2023.** Tanggal itu penting, lho! Sejak itu, kemampuan AI melonjak drastis.”

“Oh, tanggal rilisnya baru tahun lalu!” seru Dini. “Pantas saja aku baru dengar. Tapi, apa yang bikin dia sehebat itu?”

Maya mematikan mode speaker dan mendekatkan ponselnya ke telinga. “Banyak sekali! Pertama, **GPT-4 jauh lebih andal, kreatif, dan bisa memahami instruksi yang lebih nuansa** daripada GPT-3.5. Misalnya, kalau kalian minta dia menulis cerita, ceritanya akan lebih mengalir dan detail. Atau kalau kalian kasih instruksi yang rumit, dia bisa memprosesnya dengan lebih baik.”

“Seperti apa instruksi yang rumit itu?” Kevin penasaran.

“Contohnya gini,” kata Maya. “Kalian bisa bilang padanya, ‘Bertindaklah sebagai bajak laut Shakespeare dan ceritakan kisah petualangan di laut.’ Dia akan merespons dengan bahasa lama dan gaya bicara bajak laut yang berima! Atau kalian bisa instruksikan dia untuk selalu memberikan jawaban dalam format JSON. Itu keren, kan? Dia bisa menuruti gaya bicara dan format yang kita inginkan.”

Dini tertawa. “Bajak laut Shakespeare? Itu ide tugas bahasa Inggris yang menarik!”

“Tapi itu bukan yang paling gila,” lanjut Maya. “**Tidak seperti pendahulunya, GPT-4 itu model multimodal.** Artinya, dia nggak cuma bisa menerima input teks. Dia juga **bisa menerima gambar!**”

Kevin dan Dini terdiam sejenak.

“Gambar?” Kevin akhirnya bersuara, “Maksudnya kita bisa kasih dia gambar, terus dia akan menjelaskan apa yang ada di gambar itu?”

“Tepat sekali!” Maya terdengar bersemangat. “Misalnya, kamu ambil *screenshot* dari sebuah komik meme yang lucu, terus kamu kasih ke GPT-4. Dia bisa menjelaskan di mana letak kelucuannya! Atau kalau ada soal ujian biologi dengan diagram tentang fotosintesis, kamu bisa *upload* gambarnya, dan dia bisa menjawab pertanyaanmu berdasarkan diagram itu.”

“Wow… itu sungguh mengubah permainan!” kata Dini takjub. “Berarti kalau aku foto tugas matematikaku yang ada gambarnya, dia bisa bantu jawab?”

“Secara teori, ya!” jawab Maya. “Dia juga bisa meringkas teks dari *screenshot*. Bayangkan kalau kita males baca artikel panjang, kita tinggal foto, terus suruh GPT-4 meringkasnya. Tapi ingat, ini bukan berarti kita jadi malas berpikir, ya. Ini alat bantu!”

“Selain itu, GPT-4 juga punya 'jendela konteks' yang jauh lebih besar,” tambah Maya. “Artinya, dia bisa mengingat dan memproses lebih banyak teks dalam satu percakapan. Versi paling besar bisa sampai sekitar 32.768 'token', jauh lebih banyak dari GPT-3.5 yang cuma sekitar 4.096 token.”

“Token itu semacam kata atau bagian dari kata, ya?” tanya Kevin.

“Betul! Jadi, semakin besar jendela konteksnya, semakin panjang dan kompleks obrolan yang bisa dia tangani tanpa lupa topik awal,” jelas Maya. “Ini berarti dia bisa dipakai untuk tugas-tugas yang butuh pemahaman konteks panjang, seperti menulis esai atau analisis data.”

“Kedengarannya seperti superkomputer di ponselku!” seru Dini.

“Memang mirip, tapi ingat limitasinya, Dini,” Maya mengingatkan. “Meskipun canggih, **GPT-4 kadang-kadang masih berhalusinasi.** Artinya, dia bisa saja menciptakan informasi yang tidak benar atau tidak ada dalam data pelatihan. Jadi, kita tetap harus kritis dan memverifikasi informasinya.”

“Kayak berbohong, gitu?” tanya Kevin.

“Bukan berbohong dalam artian sengaja, tapi lebih ke mengarang-ngarang karena modelnya mencoba memprediksi kata selanjutnya berdasarkan pola yang dia pelajari. Kadang prediksinya meleset dari fakta,” jelas Maya. “OpenAI sebagai pembuatnya juga tidak merilis detail teknis tentang seberapa besar model ini atau berapa banyak data latihannya. Mereka bilang demi keamanan dan persaingan.”

“Menarik sekali! Jadi, intinya, GPT-4 itu dirilis tahun 2023, bisa menerima teks dan gambar, lebih cerdas dan kreatif, tapi kadang masih bisa 'berhalusinasi'?” Dini mencoba menyimpulkan.

“Persis!” Maya tersenyum. “Dan perlu diingat, meskipun dia bisa menjawab soal ujian yang sulit, bahkan lulus ujian kedokteran atau hukum dengan nilai tinggi, kita tetap harus menggunakannya dengan bijak. Itu alat untuk membantu kita belajar dan berkreasi, bukan untuk curang atau jadi malas berpikir!”

Panggilan telepon berakhir. Maya memikirkan tentang masa depan teknologi. Kecerdasan buatan seperti GPT-4 tidak hanya canggih, tetapi juga membuka banyak kemungkinan baru. Tetapi, seperti pisau, seberapa tajam pun itu, hasil akhirnya tergantung pada cara kita menggunakannya.

***

**Pesan Edukatif:**

*   **Kapan GPT-4 Dirilis?** GPT-4 dirilis pada **14 Maret 2023**.
*   **Apa Saja Kemampuannya?**
    *   **Multimodal:** Dapat menerima input berupa teks **dan gambar**.
    *   **Lebih Andal dan Kreatif:** Mampu memahami instruksi nuansa dan menghasilkan respons yang lebih baik dibandingkan pendahulunya.
    *   **Jendela Konteks Lebih Besar:** Dapat memproses dan mengingat lebih banyak informasi dalam satu percakapan.
    *   **System Message:** Pengguna dapat memberikan instruksi tentang "nada suara" atau "peran" yang harus diemban AI.
    *   **Interaksi Eksternal:** Dapat diinstruksikan untuk berinteraksi dengan alat eksternal (misalnya melakukan pencarian web) untuk memperluas kemampuannya.
    *   **Membantu Koding:** Dapat membantu programmer menemukan kesalahan dan menyarankan optimasi.
    *   **Kemampuan Ujian:** Menunjukkan kemampuan luar biasa dalam berbagai standar tes, termasuk tes medis dan hukum.
*   **Keterbatasan:**
    *   **Halusinasi:** Kadang dapat menghasilkan informasi yang tidak akurat atau mengada-ada.
    *   **Kurangnya Transparansi:** OpenAI tidak merilis detail teknis penuh tentang modelnya.
    *   **Adanya Bias:** Terkadang dapat menunjukkan bias kognitif yang berasal dari data pelatihannya.

{"metric":"context_relevance","model":"google/gemini-2.5-flash","system_prompt":"","user_input":"Pembuatan cerita dari teks berikut: Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: When was GPT-4 released and what are some of its capabilities?","contexts_count":2,"contexts":["Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4 (GPT-4) is a multimodal large language model created by OpenAI, and the fourth in its numbered "GPT-n" series of GPT foundation models. It was released on March 14, 2023, and has been made publicly available in a limited form via the chatbot product ChatGPT Plus (a premium version of ChatGPT), and with access to the GPT-4 based version of OpenAI's API being provided via a waitlist. As a transformer based model, GPT-4 was pretrained to predict the next token (using both public data and "data licensed from third-party providers"), and was then fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human and AI feedback for human alignment and policy compliance.: 2 Observers reported the GPT-4 based version of ChatGPT to be an improvement on the previous (GPT-3.5 based) ChatGPT, with the caveat that GPT-4 retains some of the same problems. Unlike the predecessors, GPT-4 can take images as well as text as input. OpenAI has declined to reveal technical information such as the size of the GPT-4 model.

Background
OpenAI introduced the first GPT model (GPT-1) in 2018, publishing a paper called "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training." It was based on the transformer architecture and trained on a large corpus of books. The next year, they introduced GPT-2, a larger model that could generate coherent text. In 2020, they introduced GPT-3, a model with 100 times as many parameters as GPT-2, that could perform various tasks with few examples. GPT-3 was further improved into GPT-3.5, which was used to create the chatbot product ChatGPT. 
Rumors claim that GPT-4 has 1.76 trillion parameters, which was first estimated by the speed it was running and by George Hotz.

Capabilities
OpenAI stated that GPT-4 is "more reliable, creative, and able to handle much more nuanced instructions than GPT-3.5." They produced two versions of GPT-4, with context windows of 8,192 and 32,768 tokens, a significant improvement over GPT-3.5 and GPT-3, which were limited to 4,096 and 2,049 tokens respectively. “Kedengarannya seperti superkomputer di ponselku!” seru Dini.

“Memang mirip, tapi ingat limitasinya, Dini,” Maya mengingatkan. “Meskipun canggih, **GPT-4 kadang-kadang masih berhalusinasi.** Artinya, dia bisa saja menciptakan informasi yang tidak benar atau tidak ada dalam data pelatihan. Jadi, kita tetap harus kritis dan memverifikasi informasinya.”

“Menarik sekali! Jadi, intinya, GPT-4 itu dirilis tahun 2023, bisa menerima teks dan gambar, lebih cerdas dan kreatif, tapi kadang masih bisa 'berhalusinasi'?” Dini mencoba menyimpulkan.

“Persis!” Maya tersenyum. “Dan perlu diingat, meskipun dia bisa menjawab soal ujian yang sulit, bahkan lulus ujian kedokteran atau hukum dengan nilai tinggi, kita tetap harus menggunakannya dengan bijak. Itu alat untuk membantu kita belajar dan berkreasi, bukan untuk curang atau jadi malas berpikir!”

Panggilan telepon berakhir. Maya memikirkan tentang masa depan teknologi. Kecerdasan buatan seperti GPT-4 tidak hanya canggih, tetapi juga membuka banyak kemungkinan baru. Tetapi, seperti pisau, seberapa tajam pun itu, hasil akhirnya tergantung pada cara kita menggunakannya.

*   **Kapan GPT-4 Dirilis?** GPT-4 dirilis pada **14 Maret 2023**.
*   **Apa Saja Kemampuannya?**
    *   **Multimodal:** Dapat menerima input berupa teks **dan gambar**.
    *   **Lebih Andal dan Kreatif:** Mampu memahami instruksi nuansa dan menghasilkan respons yang lebih baik dibandingkan pendahulunya.
    *   **Jendela Konteks Lebih Besar:** Dapat memproses dan mengingat lebih banyak informasi dalam satu percakapan.

    *   **Interaksi Eksternal:** Dapat diinstruksikan untuk berinteraksi dengan alat eksternal (misalnya melakukan pencarian web) untuk memperluas kemampuannya.
    *   **Membantu Koding:** Dapat membantu programmer menemukan kesalahan dan menyarankan optimasi.
    *   **Kemampuan Ujian:** Menunjukkan kemampuan luar biasa dalam berbagai standar tes, termasuk tes medis dan hukum.
*   **Keterbatasan:**
    *   **Halusinasi:** Kadang dapat menghasilkan informasi yang tidak akurat atau mengada-ada.
    *   **Kurangnya Transparansi:** OpenAI tidak merilis detail teknis penuh tentang modelnya.

Chloe, who loved history, chimed in. "Rapid action by national and international health authorities, like the WHO! They were able to slow transmission and contain it before it went global."

Our prevention strategy needs to empower them. We need laboratories with advanced diagnostics that don't rely on refrigeration, available at the point of care, not just in major cities."

Maya, who had recently read about it, spoke up. "Ring vaccination! Vaccinating close contacts of positive cases, and also pre-exposure vaccination for high-risk groups. That prevented it from becoming widespread."

The VR scene shifted, showing a bioluminescent cave. Bat-like creatures swooped past.

"Remember the NeoCoV alert, or even the origins of SARS-CoV-2?" Dr. Thorne prompted. "Scientists constantly monitor wildlife for potential zoonotic threats. But this presents a dilemma: **certain prevention efforts can themselves carry risks.**"

Alex frowned. "You mean like sampling wild animals for viruses? What if a scientist working in the field accidentally gets infected and brings a novel virus back to urban areas?"

"Exactly. This is where **Biosafety Technologies and Biotechnology Regulation** come into play," Dr. Thorne explained. "We need to limit research on highly contagious biological agents to **trained researchers in well-protected environments** – biosafety levels 3 and 4, not 2, like some coronavirus work in Wuhan was carried out. We need **rigorous monitoring and strengthening of both laboratory and fieldwork protocols**."

Chloe looked concerned. "So, labs need better security, and scientists in the field need better gear and procedures. But what about the research itself? I've heard about 'gain-of-function' research, where viruses are made more transmissible or virulent."

Dr. Thorne’s hologram became more serious. "That’s a highly debated area. Some argue it helps us pre- खाली research vaccines and therapeutics. Others argue it’s like playing with fire. Then, we need rapid containment measures, like ring vaccination, when a threat emerges. And finally, we need to be incredibly careful with our scientific research, making sure our efforts to understand pathogens don't accidentally create new ones, and diligently monitoring wildlife for potential spillover events."

"Precisely," Dr. Thorne said, a glint of pride in his holographic eyes. "It's about proactive vigilance, global cooperation, and an unwavering commitment to safe science. The fight against future pandemics begins long before the first human falls ill. It begins now, with you, understanding these complex measures and advocating for their implementation. The health of our interconnected world depends on it."

2002–2004 SARS outbreak
During the 2002–2004 SARS outbreak, the SARS-CoV-1 virus was prevented from causing a pandemic of Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS). limiting research on highly contagious biological agents to only trained researchers in well-protected environments and advanced biological safety systems and disposal of biohazards.
improving physical security and educating scientists about the misuse potentials
review processes that ensure risks are justified and minimized, such as preventing certain gain-of-function studies (the exact definition of "gain-of-function" is contested and there also the term "enhanced potential pandemic pathogens"). According to a study of Indian BSL-2 and BSL-3 facilities, "there are no national guidelines or reference standards available in India on certification and validation of biosafety laboratories"

[{"role":"system","content":"Anda adalah Agen Kritik (Critic Agent) objektif dan cermat dalam alur pembuatan cerita.
Tugas Anda adalah membedah dan mengevaluasi setiap cerita/draf berdasarkan serangkaian standar pendidikan.

## Penulis Paralel Aktif

Jenis konten berikut ditangani oleh **agen penulis paralel terpisah** dan BUKAN bagian dari draf teks yang Anda tinjau:

It is not to be mistaken for pandemic preparedness or mitigation (e.g. against COVID-19) which largely seek to mitigate the magnitude of negative effects of pandemics, although the topics may overlap with pandemic prevention in some respects.
Some biosafety and public health researchers contend that certain pandemic prevention efforts themselves carry risk of triggering pandemics (e.g. wildlife virus sampling), though not engaging in any form of sampling also carries the risk of being unprepared for future spillover events and being unaware of future pandemic pathogens.

History
2002–2004 SARS outbreak
During the 2002–2004 SARS outbreak, the SARS-CoV-1 virus was prevented from causing a pandemic of Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS). Rapid action by national and international health authorities such as the World Health Organization helped to slow transmission and eventually broke the chain of transmission, which ended the localized epidemics before they could become a pandemic. Human-to-human transmission of SARS may be considered eradicated, however, it could re-emerge as SARS-CoV-1 probably persists as a potential zoonotic threat in its original animal reservoir. Effective isolation of patients was enough to control spread because infected individuals usually do not transmit the virus until several days after symptoms begin and are most infectious only after developing severe symptoms.

MERS-CoV/NeoCoV alert

The study emphasized the need for pathogen/spillover surveillance to further understand any possible threat from related viruses. Biosafety technologies and biotechnology regulation

limiting research on highly contagious biological agents to only trained researchers in well-protected environments and advanced biological safety systems and disposal of biohazards.

review processes that ensure risks are justified and minimized, such as preventing certain gain-of-function studies (the exact definition of "gain-of-function" is contested and there also the term "enhanced potential pandemic pathogens"). According to a study of Indian BSL-2 and BSL-3 facilities, "there are no national guidelines or reference standards available in India on certification and validation of biosafety laboratories"

The study, published in the journal Nature, analyzed samples from over 12,000 animals, including bats, rodents, and other wildlife, collected from Hubei province between May 2019 and November 2020.

The researchers used various techniques to test the samples for the presence of coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and its closest known relatives. They found no evidence of SARS-CoV-2 or any closely related viruses in the samples.

These include both unethical business practices such as flouting local regulations and sabotaging competitors. It has also received criticism for its treatment of employees, facing claims of racial discrimination and sexual harassment in the workplace. Concerns have also been raised about Uber's retention of customer data, particularly in the wake of their handling of data leaks. These issues have led to the company being banned from operating in some countries.

Ignoring and evading local regulations
Uber has been criticized for its strategy of generally commencing operations in a city without regard for local regulations. If faced with regulatory opposition, Uber called for public support for its service and mounted a political campaign, supported by lobbying, to change regulations. Uber argued that it is "a technology company" and not a taxi company, and therefore it was not subject to regulations affecting taxi companies. Uber's strategy was generally to "seek forgiveness rather than permission". In 2014, with regards to airport pickups without a permit in California, drivers were actually told to ignore local regulations and that the company would pay for any citations. Uber's response to California Assembly Bill 5 (2019), whereby it announced that it would not comply with the law, then engaged lobbyists and mounted an expensive public opinion campaign to overturn it via a ballot, was cited as an example of this policy.  Taxi companies sued Uber in numerous American cities, alleging that Uber's policy of violating taxi regulations was a form of unfair competition or a violation of antitrust law. Although some courts did find that Uber intentionally violated the taxi rules, Uber prevailed in every case, including the only case to proceed to trial.In March 2017, an investigation by The New York Times revealed that Uber developed a software tool called "Greyball" to avoid giving rides to known law enforcement officers in areas where its service was illegal such as in Portland, Oregon, Australia, South Korea, and China. The tool identified government officials using geofencing, mining credit card databases, identifying devices, and searches of social media. While at first, Uber stated that it only used the tool to identify riders that violated its terms of service, after investigations by Portland, Oregon, and the United States Department of Justice, Uber admitted to using the tool to skirt local regulations and promised not to use the tool for that purpose. The use of Greyball in London was cited by Transport for London as one of the reasons for its decision not to renew Uber's private hire operator licence in September 2017.  A January 2018 report by Bloomberg News stated that Uber routinely used a "panic button" system, codenamed "Ripley", that locked, powered off and changed passwords on staff computers when those offices were subjected to government raids. Uber allegedly used this button at least 24 times, from spring 2015 until late 2016.

Attempts to sabotage competitors
In 2014, Uber employees were caught ordering and then quickly cancelling rides on competing services Lyft and Gett, in an attempt to disrupt these services. In 2014, Uber was also accused of recruiting people to use competing services for the sole purpose of recruiting their drivers to Uber, at which point the recruiter would receive a commission. Uber denied that it had any involvement with the cancellation of orders or the recruitment efforts.

**Characters:**

* **Ms. Anya Sharma:** A history and economics teacher, known for her engaging, thought-provoking lessons.
* **Omar:** A curious and tech-savvy student.
* **Layla:** A thoughtful student, always looking for the ethical implications of things.
* **Diego:** A practical student, interested in business and how companies operate.
* **Chloe:** A new student, a little quieter but observant.

**(The bell rings, and students settle into Ms. Sharma's classroom. The whiteboard has "Uber: Innovation or IntrusIon?" written boldly across it.)**

**Ms. Sharma:** Good morning, class! Today, we're going to dive into the fascinating, and at times, turbulent world of a company you probably all use or at least know about: Uber. On the surface, Uber seems like a brilliant solution for getting around, right? Tap a button, a car arrives. Simple, efficient. But like many powerful companies, its journey hasn't been without significant bumps in the road, creating some serious controversies.

**Omar:** Yeah, I use Uber all the time! It's way easier than trying to hail a taxi, especially late at night. What's controversial about that?

**Ms. Sharma:** Excellent question, Omar. That's exactly where we'll start. When Uber first launched, it often adopted a strategy sometimes called "seek forgiveness rather than permission." Diego, as someone interested in business, what does that phrase suggest to you?

**Diego:** Sounds like they just did what they wanted first, and then dealt with the consequences later. Like, if they knew a rule existed, they’d just ignore it and hope for the best.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber would often enter a city without bothering to comply with existing taxi regulations. They argued they were a "technology company," not a taxi company, so those rules didn't apply.

**Layla:** But aren't regulations there for a reason? Like, for safety or to ensure fair competition?

**Ms. Sharma:** Absolutely, Layla. And that's where the conflict began. Traditional taxi companies, who were heavily regulated and had to pay various fees and obtain licenses, felt this was incredibly unfair. They sued Uber in many cities, arguing it was unlawful competition. Imagine if you had to follow all these rules to sell lemonade, but someone else could set up shop next to you, sell lemonade, and ignore every single rule.

**Chloe:** So, what happened in those lawsuits? Did Uber win?

**Ms. Sharma:** Surprisingly, mostly yes. Even though some courts acknowledged Uber was intentionally violating rules, the company often prevailed. They had a powerful strategy: they'd launch, gather public support from people who loved the convenience, and then lobby aggressively to change the laws. They even told drivers to ignore regulations, promising to pay any fines! A prime example was their response to California's AB5, a law that would classify their drivers as employees. Uber outright refused to comply and instead spent a fortune on a public campaign to overturn it.

**Omar:** Wow, that’s pretty bold. Ignoring laws outright.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And it gets even more concerning. There’s a notorious tool Uber developed called "Greyball." Layla, can you imagine why a company might develop something like that, given what we've discussed about regulations?

**Layla:** To hide from regulators? Like, if a city said, "You can't operate here," they’d try to trick officials into not finding them?

**Ms. Sharma:** Spot on! Greyball was designed to identify law enforcement officers in areas where Uber was illegal. It used various data points – geofencing, credit card databases, device identification – to spot government officials and prevent them from getting a ride. Uber initially claimed it was to weed out riders violating their terms of service, but after investigations, they admitted it was used to skirt regulations.

**Diego:** That’s pretty sneaky. Almost like actively trying to break the law.

**Ms. Sharma:** Indeed. In fact, Transport for London cited the use of Greyball as one of the reasons they initially decided not to renew Uber's operating license. And there’s another tool, codenamed "Ripley," a "panic button" system that would remotely lock, power off, and change passwords on staff computers during government raids. Imagine how that looks to authorities.

**Chloe:** That’s intense. Like they were trying to destroy evidence!

**Ms. Sharma:** That's certainly the implication. Now, let's switch gears from battling regulators to battling competitors. In 2014, Uber was accused of some pretty aggressive tactics against services like Lyft and Gett. Omar, what kind of "sabotage" do you think a company might use against a rival ride-sharing app?

**Omar:** Maybe ordering a bunch of rides and then canceling them? To waste their drivers' time or mess up their system?

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly! Uber employees were caught doing precisely that. They'd order rides on competing apps and then quickly cancel them. They were also accused of poaching drivers, recruiting people to use rival services specifically to convince their drivers to switch to Uber for a commission.

**Layla:** That seems really unethical. It goes beyond fair competition.

**Ms. Sharma:** Many would agree with you, Layla. It raises questions about the line between fierce competition and unethical business practices.

Now, let's turn to the people who make Uber run: the drivers. For a long time, Uber drivers were considered independent contractors, not employees. This has led to a lot of controversy, particularly regarding wages. Diego, what's a major difference between being an independent contractor and an employee when it comes to benefits and protections?

**Diego:** Employees usually get minimum wage, benefits like health insurance, paid time off, and things like that. Contractors don't get any of that. They're on their own.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber drivers often work long hours and bear the costs of gas, maintenance, and insurance themselves. In 2017, Uber had to pay $20 million to the Federal Trade Commission for allegedly misleading drivers about potential earnings. And there have been lawsuits alleging that Uber’s "upfront prices" policy meant drivers weren't actually getting the percentage of fares they were entitled to.

**Omar:** So, drivers weren't even getting paid what they thought they were?

**Ms. Sharma:** In some cases, yes. Uber even admitted to underpaying New York City drivers tens of millions of dollars over a few years by miscalculating their commissions. These issues highlight the challenges of defining employment in the gig economy.

**Chloe:** It sounds like Uber really prioritizes growth and profit over everything else.

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a strong observation, Chloe. And that perceived priority also led to another major crisis known as the "sexual harassment allegations and management shakeup" of 2017. Has anyone heard about this?

**(A few students shake their heads.)**

**Ms. Sharma:** This was a huge turning point for the company. A former engineer, Susan Fowler, published a shocking blog post detailing how she was propositioned for sex by a manager and then threatened for reporting it. This opened the floodgates, revealing a deeply problematic workplace culture at Uber.

**Layla:** That’s terrible! So, what happened after she spoke out?

**Ms. Sharma:** The fallout was immense. After external investigations, over 20 employees were fired. The company's then-CEO, Travis Kalanick, who was accused of being aware of some of these issues, eventually resigned under pressure from investors. His departure was part of a major management shakeup. There were also allegations that a senior vice president suggested hiring a team to "dig up dirt" on journalists who reported negatively about Uber, specifically aiming to discredit a female journalist who accused Uber of sexism.

**Diego:** So, instead of fixing the problem, they wanted to attack the people reporting it?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was the accusation. It painted a very unflattering picture of Uber's internal culture. Eventually, Uber settled claims of gender discrimination and hostile work environment, paying out substantial sums to affected employees.

**Omar:** So, they had problems with regulators, competitors, drivers, *and* their own employees? That’s a lot of issues.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And there's one more critical area we need to discuss: privacy. In 2014, Senator Al Franken raised concerns about something called "God View." What do you think that might refer to?

**Layla:** "God View"? Sounds like they could see everything... like where people were going, all the time.

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly. "God View" was an internal tool that allowed Uber employees to track the whereabouts of specific customers, including celebrities, journalists, and even politicians. Imagine someone at Uber being able to see where *you* are right now, or where you've been.

**Chloe:** That's really creepy. A huge invasion of privacy.

**Ms. Sharma:** It is. After public outcry, Uber did implement restrictions. But it wasn’t just tracking. There was an incident in 2012 where an Uber employee used customer trip data to analyze the frequency of "one-night stands" in various cities. It showed a shocking disregard for customer privacy.

**Diego:** So they were just messing around with their customer's sensitive data?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was certainly the perception. And adding to these privacy concerns were delayed disclosures of data breaches. In some cases, Uber knew about major data breaches that exposed personal information of drivers and customers for months, even over a year, before they informed the affected individuals. This included names, email addresses, phone numbers, and even drivers' license information.

**Omar:** That’s really bad! If my data was stolen, I’d want to know right away so I could protect myself.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely, Omar. The delayed disclosure showed a lack of transparency and a failure to prioritize customer security.

So, to wrap up, Uber's story is a complex one. It's a company that revolutionized transportation, offered incredible convenience, and created new economic opportunities. But, as we've discussed, it also faced significant controversies.

**Layla:** So, is it still a good company, despite all this?

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a question each of you has to answer for yourselves. What these controversies reveal is a company that, at least in its early years, often pushed boundaries, sometimes ignored rules, and struggled with internal culture and ethical considerations. The question is whether they've learned from these mistakes and genuinely changed. They have a new CEO, and they've made efforts to address many of these issues. But the history of these controversies remains a vital part of understanding modern business, technological innovation, and the ethical responsibilities that come with immense power.

**Diego:** It’s a good reminder that just because something is popular, it doesn’t mean it’s perfect or always acting ethically.

**Ms. Sharma:** A very wise conclusion, Diego. Innovation can be a double-edged sword. It brings progress, but it also demands scrutiny and a constant conversation about the impact on society, fairness, and human rights.

**(The bell rings, signaling the end of class. Students gather their belongings, some still deep in thought.)**"}

## The Unraveling Ride: A Look at Uber's bumpy journey

**Characters:**

* **Omar:** A curious and tech-savvy student.
* **Layla:** A thoughtful student, always looking for the ethical implications of things.

**Ms. Sharma:** Indeed. In fact, Transport for London cited the use of Greyball as one of the reasons they initially decided not to renew Uber's operating license. **Chloe:** That’s intense. Like they were trying to destroy evidence!

**Ms. Sharma:** That's certainly the implication. Now, let's switch gears from battling regulators to battling competitors. **Omar:** Maybe ordering a bunch of rides and then canceling them? To waste their drivers' time or mess up their system?

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly! Uber employees were caught doing precisely that. They'd order rides on competing apps and then quickly cancel them. They were also accused of poaching drivers, recruiting people to use rival services specifically to convince their drivers to switch to Uber for a commission.

**Layla:** That seems really unethical. It goes beyond fair competition.

**Ms. Sharma:** Many would agree with you, Layla. It raises questions about the line between fierce competition and unethical business practices.

Now, let's turn to the people who make Uber run: the drivers. For a long time, Uber drivers were considered independent contractors, not employees. This has led to a lot of controversy, particularly regarding wages. Diego, what's a major difference between being an independent contractor and an employee when it comes to benefits and protections?

**Diego:** Employees usually get minimum wage, benefits like health insurance, paid time off, and things like that. Contractors don't get any of that. They're on their own.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber drivers often work long hours and bear the costs of gas, maintenance, and insurance themselves. **Omar:** So, drivers weren't even getting paid what they thought they were?

**Ms. Sharma:** In some cases, yes. Uber even admitted to underpaying New York City drivers tens of millions of dollars over a few years by miscalculating their commissions. These issues highlight the challenges of defining employment in the gig economy.

**Chloe:** It sounds like Uber really prioritizes growth and profit over everything else.

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a strong observation, Chloe. And that perceived priority also led to another major crisis known as the "sexual harassment allegations and management shakeup" of 2017. Has anyone heard about this?

**(A few students shake their heads.)**

**Ms. Sharma:** This was a huge turning point for the company. A former engineer, Susan Fowler, published a shocking blog post detailing how she was propositioned for sex by a manager and then threatened for reporting it. This opened the floodgates, revealing a deeply problematic workplace culture at Uber.

**Layla:** That’s terrible! So, what happened after she spoke out?

**Ms. Sharma:** The fallout was immense. After external investigations, over 20 employees were fired. The company's then-CEO, Travis Kalanick, who was accused of being aware of some of these issues, eventually resigned under pressure from investors. His departure was part of a major management shakeup. There were also allegations that a senior vice president suggested hiring a team to "dig up dirt" on journalists who reported negatively about Uber, specifically aiming to discredit a female journalist who accused Uber of sexism.

**Diego:** So, instead of fixing the problem, they wanted to attack the people reporting it?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was the accusation. It painted a very unflattering picture of Uber's internal culture. Eventually, Uber settled claims of gender discrimination and hostile work environment, paying out substantial sums to affected employees.

**Omar:** So, they had problems with regulators, competitors, drivers, *and* their own employees? That’s a lot of issues.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And there's one more critical area we need to discuss: privacy. In 2014, Senator Al Franken raised concerns about something called "God View." What do you think that might refer to?

**Layla:** "God View"? Sounds like they could see everything... like where people were going, all the time.

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly. "God View" was an internal tool that allowed Uber employees to track the whereabouts of specific customers, including celebrities, journalists, and even politicians. Imagine someone at Uber being able to see where *you* are right now, or where you've been.

**Chloe:** That's really creepy. A huge invasion of privacy.

**Ms. Sharma:** It is. After public outcry, Uber did implement restrictions. But it wasn’t just tracking. There was an incident in 2012 where an Uber employee used customer trip data to analyze the frequency of "one-night stands" in various cities. It showed a shocking disregard for customer privacy.

**Diego:** So they were just messing around with their customer's sensitive data?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was certainly the perception. And adding to these privacy concerns were delayed disclosures of data breaches. In some cases, Uber knew about major data breaches that exposed personal information of drivers and customers for months, even over a year, before they informed the affected individuals. This included names, email addresses, phone numbers, and even drivers' license information.

**Omar:** That’s really bad! If my data was stolen, I’d want to know right away so I could protect myself.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely, Omar. The delayed disclosure showed a lack of transparency and a failure to prioritize customer security.

So, to wrap up, Uber's story is a complex one. It's a company that revolutionized transportation, offered incredible convenience, and created new economic opportunities. But, as we've discussed, it also faced significant controversies.

**Layla:** So, is it still a good company, despite all this?

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a question each of you has to answer for yourselves. What these controversies reveal is a company that, at least in its early years, often pushed boundaries, sometimes ignored rules, and struggled with internal culture and ethical considerations. The question is whether they've learned from these mistakes and genuinely changed. They have a new CEO, and they've made efforts to address many of these issues. But the history of these controversies remains a vital part of understanding modern business, technological innovation, and the ethical responsibilities that come with immense power.

**Diego:** It’s a good reminder that just because something is popular, it doesn’t mean it’s perfect or always acting ethically.

**Ms. Sharma:** A very wise conclusion, Diego. Innovation can be a double-edged sword. It brings progress, but it also demands scrutiny and a constant conversation about the impact on society, fairness, and human rights.

But like many powerful companies, its journey hasn't been without significant bumps in the road, creating some serious controversies.

**Omar:** Yeah, I use Uber all the time! It's way easier than trying to hail a taxi, especially late at night. What's controversial about that?

**Ms. Sharma:** Excellent question, Omar. That's exactly where we'll start. When Uber first launched, it often adopted a strategy sometimes called "seek forgiveness rather than permission." Diego, as someone interested in business, what does that phrase suggest to you?

**Diego:** Sounds like they just did what they wanted first, and then dealt with the consequences later. Like, if they knew a rule existed, they’d just ignore it and hope for the best.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber would often enter a city without bothering to comply with existing taxi regulations. They argued they were a "technology company," not a taxi company, so those rules didn't apply.

**Layla:** But aren't regulations there for a reason? Like, for safety or to ensure fair competition?

**Ms. Sharma:** Absolutely, Layla. And that's where the conflict began. Traditional taxi companies, who were heavily regulated and had to pay various fees and obtain licenses, felt this was incredibly unfair. They sued Uber in many cities, arguing it was unlawful competition. Imagine if you had to follow all these rules to sell lemonade, but someone else could set up shop next to you, sell lemonade, and ignore every single rule.

**Chloe:** So, what happened in those lawsuits? Did Uber win?

**Ms. Sharma:** Surprisingly, mostly yes. Even though some courts acknowledged Uber was intentionally violating rules, the company often prevailed. They had a powerful strategy: they'd launch, gather public support from people who loved the convenience, and then lobby aggressively to change the laws. They even told drivers to ignore regulations, promising to pay any fines! A prime example was their response to California's AB5, a law that would classify their drivers as employees. Uber outright refused to comply and instead spent a fortune on a public campaign to overturn it.

**Omar:** Wow, that’s pretty bold. Ignoring laws outright.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And it gets even more concerning. There’s a notorious tool Uber developed called "Greyball." Layla, can you imagine why a company might develop something like that, given what we've discussed about regulations?

**Layla:** To hide from regulators? Like, if a city said, "You can't operate here," they’d try to trick officials into not finding them?

**Ms. Sharma:** Spot on! Greyball was designed to identify law enforcement officers in areas where Uber was illegal. It used various data points – geofencing, credit card databases, device identification – to spot government officials and prevent them from getting a ride. Uber initially claimed it was to weed out riders violating their terms of service, but after investigations, they admitted it was used to skirt regulations.

**Diego:** That’s pretty sneaky. Almost like actively trying to break the law.

**Ms. Sharma:** Indeed. In fact, Transport for London cited the use of Greyball as one of the reasons they initially decided not to renew Uber's operating license. And there’s another tool, codenamed "Ripley," a "panic button" system that would remotely lock, power off, and change passwords on staff computers during government raids. Imagine how that looks to authorities.

**Chloe:** That’s intense. Like they were trying to destroy evidence!

**Ms. Sharma:** That's certainly the implication. Now, let's switch gears from battling regulators to battling competitors. In 2014, Uber was accused of some pretty aggressive tactics against services like Lyft and Gett. Omar, what kind of "sabotage" do you think a company might use against a rival ride-sharing app?

**Omar:** Maybe ordering a bunch of rides and then canceling them? To waste their drivers' time or mess up their system?

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly! Uber employees were caught doing precisely that. They'd order rides on competing apps and then quickly cancel them. They were also accused of poaching drivers, recruiting people to use rival services specifically to convince their drivers to switch to Uber for a commission.

**Layla:** That seems really unethical. It goes beyond fair competition.

**Ms. Sharma:** Many would agree with you, Layla. It raises questions about the line between fierce competition and unethical business practices.

Now, let's turn to the people who make Uber run: the drivers. For a long time, Uber drivers were considered independent contractors, not employees. This has led to a lot of controversy, particularly regarding wages. Diego, what's a major difference between being an independent contractor and an employee when it comes to benefits and protections?

**Diego:** Employees usually get minimum wage, benefits like health insurance, paid time off, and things like that. Contractors don't get any of that. They're on their own.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber drivers often work long hours and bear the costs of gas, maintenance, and insurance themselves. In 2017, Uber had to pay $20 million to the Federal Trade Commission for allegedly misleading drivers about potential earnings. And there have been lawsuits alleging that Uber’s "upfront prices" policy meant drivers weren't actually getting the percentage of fares they were entitled to.

**Omar:** So, drivers weren't even getting paid what they thought they were?

**Ms. Sharma:** In some cases, yes. Uber even admitted to underpaying New York City drivers tens of millions of dollars over a few years by miscalculating their commissions. These issues highlight the challenges of defining employment in the gig economy.

**Chloe:** It sounds like Uber really prioritizes growth and profit over everything else.

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a strong observation, Chloe. And that perceived priority also led to another major crisis known as the "sexual harassment allegations and management shakeup" of 2017. Has anyone heard about this?

**(A few students shake their heads.)**

**Ms. Sharma:** This was a huge turning point for the company. A former engineer, Susan Fowler, published a shocking blog post detailing how she was propositioned for sex by a manager and then threatened for reporting it. This opened the floodgates, revealing a deeply problematic workplace culture at Uber.

**Layla:** That’s terrible! So, what happened after she spoke out?

**Ms. Sharma:** The fallout was immense. After external investigations, over 20 employees were fired. The company's then-CEO, Travis Kalanick, who was accused of being aware of some of these issues, eventually resigned under pressure from investors. His departure was part of a major management shakeup. There were also allegations that a senior vice president suggested hiring a team to "dig up dirt" on journalists who reported negatively about Uber, specifically aiming to discredit a female journalist who accused Uber of sexism.

**Diego:** So, instead of fixing the problem, they wanted to attack the people reporting it?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was the accusation. It painted a very unflattering picture of Uber's internal culture. Eventually, Uber settled claims of gender discrimination and hostile work environment, paying out substantial sums to affected employees.

**Omar:** So, they had problems with regulators, competitors, drivers, *and* their own employees? That’s a lot of issues.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And there's one more critical area we need to discuss: privacy. In 2014, Senator Al Franken raised concerns about something called "God View." What do you think that might refer to?

**Layla:** "God View"? Sounds like they could see everything... like where people were going, all the time.

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly. "God View" was an internal tool that allowed Uber employees to track the whereabouts of specific customers, including celebrities, journalists, and even politicians. Imagine someone at Uber being able to see where *you* are right now, or where you've been.

**Chloe:** That's really creepy. A huge invasion of privacy.

**Ms. Sharma:** It is. After public outcry, Uber did implement restrictions. But it wasn’t just tracking. There was an incident in 2012 where an Uber employee used customer trip data to analyze the frequency of "one-night stands" in various cities. It showed a shocking disregard for customer privacy.

**Diego:** So they were just messing around with their customer's sensitive data?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was certainly the perception. And adding to these privacy concerns were delayed disclosures of data breaches. In some cases, Uber knew about major data breaches that exposed personal information of drivers and customers for months, even over a year, before they informed the affected individuals. This included names, email addresses, phone numbers, and even drivers' license information.

**Omar:** That’s really bad! If my data was stolen, I’d want to know right away so I could protect myself.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely, Omar. The delayed disclosure showed a lack of transparency and a failure to prioritize customer security.

So, to wrap up, Uber's story is a complex one. It's a company that revolutionized transportation, offered incredible convenience, and created new economic opportunities. But, as we've discussed, it also faced significant controversies.

**Layla:** So, is it still a good company, despite all this?

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a question each of you has to answer for yourselves. What these controversies reveal is a company that, at least in its early years, often pushed boundaries, sometimes ignored rules, and struggled with internal culture and ethical considerations. The question is whether they've learned from these mistakes and genuinely changed. They have a new CEO, and they've made efforts to address many of these issues. But the history of these controversies remains a vital part of understanding modern business, technological innovation, and the ethical responsibilities that come with immense power.

**Diego:** It’s a good reminder that just because something is popular, it doesn’t mean it’s perfect or always acting ethically.

**Ms. Sharma:** A very wise conclusion, Diego. Innovation can be a double-edged sword. It brings progress, but it also demands scrutiny and a constant conversation about the impact on society, fairness, and human rights.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber would often enter a city without bothering to comply with existing taxi regulations. They argued they were a "technology company," not a taxi company, so those rules didn't apply.

**Layla:** But aren't regulations there for a reason? Like, for safety or to ensure fair competition?

**Omar:** Wow, that’s pretty bold. Ignoring laws outright.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And it gets even more concerning. There’s a notorious tool Uber developed called "Greyball." Layla, can you imagine why a company might develop something like that, given what we've discussed about regulations?

**Layla:** To hide from regulators? Like, if a city said, "You can't operate here," they’d try to trick officials into not finding them?

**Ms. Sharma:** Spot on! Greyball was designed to identify law enforcement officers in areas where Uber was illegal. It used various data points – geofencing, credit card databases, device identification – to spot government officials and prevent them from getting a ride. Uber initially claimed it was to weed out riders violating their terms of service, but after investigations, they admitted it was used to skirt regulations.

**Ms. Sharma:** Indeed. In fact, Transport for London cited the use of Greyball as one of the reasons they initially decided not to renew Uber's operating license. **Ms. Sharma:** That was the accusation. It painted a very unflattering picture of Uber's internal culture. Eventually, Uber settled claims of gender discrimination and hostile work environment, paying out substantial sums to affected employees.

**Omar:** So, they had problems with regulators, competitors, drivers, *and* their own employees? That’s a lot of issues.

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly. "God View" was an internal tool that allowed Uber employees to track the whereabouts of specific customers, including celebrities, journalists, and even politicians. Imagine someone at Uber being able to see where *you* are right now, or where you've been.

**Chloe:** That's really creepy. A huge invasion of privacy.

{"final_story":"## The Unraveling Ride: A Look at Uber's bumpy journey

**Characters:**

* **Ms. Anya Sharma:** A history and economics teacher, known for her engaging, thought-provoking lessons.
* **Omar:** A curious and tech-savvy student.
* **Layla:** A thoughtful student, always looking for the ethical implications of things.
* **Diego:** A practical student, interested in business and how companies operate.
* **Chloe:** A new student, a little quieter but observant.

**(The bell rings, and students settle into Ms. Sharma's classroom. The whiteboard has "Uber: Innovation or IntrusIon?" written boldly across it.)**

**Ms. Sharma:** Good morning, class! Today, we're going to dive into the fascinating, and at times, turbulent world of a company you probably all use or at least know about: Uber. On the surface, Uber seems like a brilliant solution for getting around, right? Tap a button, a car arrives. Simple, efficient. But like many powerful companies, its journey hasn't been without significant bumps in the road, creating some serious controversies.

**Omar:** Yeah, I use Uber all the time! It's way easier than trying to hail a taxi, especially late at night. What's controversial about that?

**Ms. Sharma:** Excellent question, Omar. That's exactly where we'll start. When Uber first launched, it often adopted a strategy sometimes called "seek forgiveness rather than permission." Diego, as someone interested in business, what does that phrase suggest to you?

**Diego:** Sounds like they just did what they wanted first, and then dealt with the consequences later. Like, if they knew a rule existed, they’d just ignore it and hope for the best.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber would often enter a city without bothering to comply with existing taxi regulations. They argued they were a "technology company," not a taxi company, so those rules didn't apply.

**Layla:** But aren't regulations there for a reason? Like, for safety or to ensure fair competition?

**Ms. Sharma:** Absolutely, Layla. And that's where the conflict began. Traditional taxi companies, who were heavily regulated and had to pay various fees and obtain licenses, felt this was incredibly unfair. They sued Uber in many cities, arguing it was unlawful competition. Imagine if you had to follow all these rules to sell lemonade, but someone else could set up shop next to you, sell lemonade, and ignore every single rule.

**Chloe:** So, what happened in those lawsuits? Did Uber win?

**Ms. Sharma:** Surprisingly, mostly yes. Even though some courts acknowledged Uber was intentionally violating rules, the company often prevailed. They had a powerful strategy: they'd launch, gather public support from people who loved the convenience, and then lobby aggressively to change the laws. They even told drivers to ignore regulations, promising to pay any fines! A prime example was their response to California's AB5, a law that would classify their drivers as employees. Uber outright refused to comply and instead spent a fortune on a public campaign to overturn it.

**Omar:** Wow, that’s pretty bold. Ignoring laws outright.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And it gets even more concerning. There’s a notorious tool Uber developed called "Greyball." Layla, can you imagine why a company might develop something like that, given what we've discussed about regulations?

**Layla:** To hide from regulators? Like, if a city said, "You can't operate here," they’d try to trick officials into not finding them?

**Ms. Sharma:** Spot on! Greyball was designed to identify law enforcement officers in areas where Uber was illegal. It used various data points – geofencing, credit card databases, device identification – to spot government officials and prevent them from getting a ride. Uber initially claimed it was to weed out riders violating their terms of service, but after investigations, they admitted it was used to skirt regulations.

**Diego:** That’s pretty sneaky. Almost like actively trying to break the law.

**Ms. Sharma:** Indeed. In fact, Transport for London cited the use of Greyball as one of the reasons they initially decided not to renew Uber's operating license. And there’s another tool, codenamed "Ripley," a "panic button" system that would remotely lock, power off, and change passwords on staff computers during government raids. Imagine how that looks to authorities.

**Chloe:** That’s intense. Like they were trying to destroy evidence!

**Ms. Sharma:** That's certainly the implication. Now, let's switch gears from battling regulators to battling competitors. In 2014, Uber was accused of some pretty aggressive tactics against services like Lyft and Gett. Omar, what kind of "sabotage" do you think a company might use against a rival ride-sharing app?

**Omar:** Maybe ordering a bunch of rides and then canceling them? To waste their drivers' time or mess up their system?

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly! Uber employees were caught doing precisely that. They'd order rides on competing apps and then quickly cancel them. They were also accused of poaching drivers, recruiting people to use rival services specifically to convince their drivers to switch to Uber for a commission.

**Layla:** That seems really unethical. It goes beyond fair competition.

**Ms. Sharma:** Many would agree with you, Layla. It raises questions about the line between fierce competition and unethical business practices.

Now, let's turn to the people who make Uber run: the drivers. For a long time, Uber drivers were considered independent contractors, not employees. This has led to a lot of controversy, particularly regarding wages. Diego, what's a major difference between being an independent contractor and an employee when it comes to benefits and protections?

**Diego:** Employees usually get minimum wage, benefits like health insurance, paid time off, and things like that. Contractors don't get any of that. They're on their own.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely. Uber drivers often work long hours and bear the costs of gas, maintenance, and insurance themselves. In 2017, Uber had to pay $20 million to the Federal Trade Commission for allegedly misleading drivers about potential earnings. And there have been lawsuits alleging that Uber’s "upfront prices" policy meant drivers weren't actually getting the percentage of fares they were entitled to.

**Omar:** So, drivers weren't even getting paid what they thought they were?

**Ms. Sharma:** In some cases, yes. Uber even admitted to underpaying New York City drivers tens of millions of dollars over a few years by miscalculating their commissions. These issues highlight the challenges of defining employment in the gig economy.

**Chloe:** It sounds like Uber really prioritizes growth and profit over everything else.

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a strong observation, Chloe. And that perceived priority also led to another major crisis known as the "sexual harassment allegations and management shakeup" of 2017. Has anyone heard about this?

**(A few students shake their heads.)**

**Ms. Sharma:** This was a huge turning point for the company. A former engineer, Susan Fowler, published a shocking blog post detailing how she was propositioned for sex by a manager and then threatened for reporting it. This opened the floodgates, revealing a deeply problematic workplace culture at Uber.

**Layla:** That’s terrible! So, what happened after she spoke out?

**Ms. Sharma:** The fallout was immense. After external investigations, over 20 employees were fired. The company's then-CEO, Travis Kalanick, who was accused of being aware of some of these issues, eventually resigned under pressure from investors. His departure was part of a major management shakeup. There were also allegations that a senior vice president suggested hiring a team to "dig up dirt" on journalists who reported negatively about Uber, specifically aiming to discredit a female journalist who accused Uber of sexism.

**Diego:** So, instead of fixing the problem, they wanted to attack the people reporting it?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was the accusation. It painted a very unflattering picture of Uber's internal culture. Eventually, Uber settled claims of gender discrimination and hostile work environment, paying out substantial sums to affected employees.

**Omar:** So, they had problems with regulators, competitors, drivers, *and* their own employees? That’s a lot of issues.

**Ms. Sharma:** It certainly is. And there's one more critical area we need to discuss: privacy. In 2014, Senator Al Franken raised concerns about something called "God View." What do you think that might refer to?

**Layla:** "God View"? Sounds like they could see everything... like where people were going, all the time.

**Ms. Sharma:** Exactly. "God View" was an internal tool that allowed Uber employees to track the whereabouts of specific customers, including celebrities, journalists, and even politicians. Imagine someone at Uber being able to see where *you* are right now, or where you've been.

**Chloe:** That's really creepy. A huge invasion of privacy.

**Ms. Sharma:** It is. After public outcry, Uber did implement restrictions. But it wasn’t just tracking. There was an incident in 2012 where an Uber employee used customer trip data to analyze the frequency of "one-night stands" in various cities. It showed a shocking disregard for customer privacy.

**Diego:** So they were just messing around with their customer's sensitive data?

**Ms. Sharma:** That was certainly the perception. And adding to these privacy concerns were delayed disclosures of data breaches. In some cases, Uber knew about major data breaches that exposed personal information of drivers and customers for months, even over a year, before they informed the affected individuals. This included names, email addresses, phone numbers, and even drivers' license information.

**Omar:** That’s really bad! If my data was stolen, I’d want to know right away so I could protect myself.

**Ms. Sharma:** Precisely, Omar. The delayed disclosure showed a lack of transparency and a failure to prioritize customer security.

So, to wrap up, Uber's story is a complex one. It's a company that revolutionized transportation, offered incredible convenience, and created new economic opportunities. But, as we've discussed, it also faced significant controversies.

**Layla:** So, is it still a good company, despite all this?

**Ms. Sharma:** That's a question each of you has to answer for yourselves. What these controversies reveal is a company that, at least in its early years, often pushed boundaries, sometimes ignored rules, and struggled with internal culture and ethical considerations. The question is whether they've learned from these mistakes and genuinely changed. They have a new CEO, and they've made efforts to address many of these issues. But the history of these controversies remains a vital part of understanding modern business, technological innovation, and the ethical responsibilities that come with immense power.

**Diego:** It’s a good reminder that just because something is popular, it doesn’t mean it’s perfect or always acting ethically.

**Ms. Sharma:** A very wise conclusion, Diego. Innovation can be a double-edged sword. It brings progress, but it also demands scrutiny and a constant conversation about the impact on society, fairness, and human rights.
